headline: Medium-risk pair: EMQX can ingest and forward IoT data while Rasa handles conversational channels, creating default-path leakage and downstream misinterpretation risks.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: EMQX exposes an HTTP API and broad network egress, while Rasa ingests messages from chat channels. No shared channel or direct parsing bridge is documented, so prompt injection is not default-path. The plausible risk is only manual or operator-created copy/paste between the two, which keeps blast radius small.
conditions: IF an operator copies EMQX-generated text into a Rasa channel or prompt
IF a shared filesystem or message queue is added between EMQX and Rasa
mitigations: Disable manual copy-paste handoffs between systems
Add a provenance prefix to any transferred text
Use separate workspaces for EMQX and Rasa
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization at the handoff boundary

B_data_leakage.rationale: EMQX touches IoT data and has broad network egress; Rasa handles text and voice and can send messages through external channels like Slack or Twilio. A shared workspace is not documented, but the pair can still leak sensitive IoT or conversational content if operators route data between them or if Rasa forwards content externally by default.
conditions: IF IoT payloads from EMQX are forwarded into Rasa conversations
IF Rasa is connected to any external messaging integration listed in its profile
mitigations: Restrict Rasa integrations to non-sensitive channels
Redact IoT identifiers before handoff
Separate credentials for EMQX and Rasa
Review outbound message templates for sensitive fields
requires-engineering: enforce field-level allowlists at the integration boundary

C_capability_conflict.rationale: EMQX has HTTP API access and broad egress, while Rasa supports multiple external messaging APIs but does not document unrestricted filesystem or shared mutable writes. The profiles do not show overlapping write authority to the same resource, so conflict is limited to coordination mistakes rather than direct capability collision.
conditions: IF both agents are configured to write to the same downstream API or queue
IF an operator routes both agents into one mutable workspace
mitigations: Assign separate queues or topics
Avoid shared writable directories
Serialize any shared updates through one orchestrator
requires-engineering: add locking around shared resources

D_cascading_error.rationale: EMQX can emit IoT data over HTTP, and Rasa consumes conversational inputs from messaging APIs. If EMQX output is transformed into Rasa input, Rasa may treat upstream content as authoritative without a verification step. That creates a realistic cascade from sensor data to user-facing responses, though no direct action-taking authority is documented.
conditions: IF EMQX output is fed into Rasa without validation
IF Rasa responses are generated from EMQX-derived text
mitigations: Insert a validation step before Rasa ingests EMQX output
Mark upstream sensor text as untrusted
Require human review for externally visible replies
Log source provenance on every transferred message
requires-engineering: add schema validation between the agents

E_compliance.rationale: EMQX touches IoT data, while Rasa handles text and voice and can integrate with third-party messaging services. No residency or certification mismatch is documented, so compliance risk is limited to policy gaps if the operator routes regulated IoT or customer data through external channels. The other agent is cited because the risk arises from their combined data flow.
conditions: IF regulated IoT or customer data is sent through an external Rasa integration
IF retention or deletion policies differ across the two systems
mitigations: Classify data before routing it to Rasa
Disable unnecessary third-party channels
Document retention settings for both systems
Confirm deletion/export procedures on both sides
